title: Tendency to Minimize Energy Output
hook: The tax folder on the desk beat the receipt drawer because it asked Louise for one motion, not five.
counterintuition: Effort follows contour. People drift toward the lower-energy path, so the useful move is to make that path serve the goal.
tryThisNow: Choose one repeated failure and remove two motions from the good path. Add those motions to the bad path before the next attempt.
keyTakeaway: Systems tend to conserve effort; design the environment so the path of least resistance carries people toward the desired action.

breakdown.fastRead:
Louise did not lose deduction receipts because she was lazy. The receipt drawer was closer than the tax folder, and filing meant finding the checklist later. The easier path scattered the documents.

She put the folder beside the door, clipped the filing checklist to the front, and moved the receipt drawer out of reach.

The tendency to minimize energy output is a path preference. When the easier route conflicts with the goal, the route usually wins.
breakdown.deepRead:
"They keep walking the long way," Brian said, watching pickers cross the warehouse again. The aisle map showed a better route. The scanner strap made the old route easier because workers could scan from the wrong side without noticing the extra steps.

The support is conservative: systems drift toward lower-effort paths, conserve effort, and prefer easier routines when constraints permit. Brian did not need to accuse workers of laziness. He needed to make the better route lower energy. The aisle map, scanner strap, and step counter had to point in the same direction. Design beats scolding when the easier path is wrong.

The default is the real instruction.

Remy saw the same pattern on tired evenings. The prep tray was empty, the recipe card required chopping, and the freezer label hid the ready ingredients. He predicted he would cook because he cared about healthy dinners. The reveal came at 7:30: effort followed the open delivery app. Moving chopped ingredients to the tray made the better dinner the easier dinner.

The limit is complacency. Lower effort can preserve useful routines, or it can trap you in convenience that drains skill, health, money, or trust. The model does not worship ease. It asks what your environment makes easiest.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 11:04 p.m., Brianna opened the notification screen after another failed study session. The practice deck was ready, but the phone lockout setting allowed every message through. Studying required choosing effort again and again. Checking the phone required no choice at all.

This is the practical force behind energy minimization. The lower-effort path does not need to win an argument. It simply waits closer, opens faster, or requires fewer steps. If the goal is uphill and the distraction is downhill, good intentions spend the whole evening fighting gravity.

Where have you made the wrong action cheaper than the right one?

That question moves the model from judgment to design. Louise did not need a lecture about responsibility. Brian did not need a warehouse speech about discipline. Remy did not need a harder recipe. Brianna did not need to prove she cared. Each needed the lower-energy route rebuilt so the desired action required less effort than the drift. The same person can look disciplined in one room and careless in another because the rooms ask for different amounts of energy.

You can feel the same issue in payroll. Samuel sees an approval queue with late invoices and a vendor email asking why payment slipped. The shortcut is one click: mark later. The better action requires opening the invoice timestamp, checking the approval queue, and replying. If the system makes delay easier than completion, late payments become predictable. Samuel changes the queue so the next valid approval is the shortest path. The design does not make him nobler; it makes the right action cheaper at the moment the choice appears.

Rafael learned it in an apartment laundry room. The lint sign was polite, the sorting shelf was crowded, and the laundry token machine stood near the exit. Neighbors left the lint trap full because cleaning it added steps after the main job felt done. He moved the lint sign to the token machine and put the small bin beside the dryer door. The lower-energy path now included the cleanup. Nobody had to become a different kind of neighbor to follow it.

Energy minimization can be humane. It respects fatigue, attention, and the fact that people are not machines. It can also be dangerous when low effort serves the wrong default. Easy can mean accessible, sustainable, and kind. Easy can also mean addictive, sloppy, or avoidant. The work is not to make life harder. The work is to aim ease.

Put friction where drift hurts you. Remove friction where the good action begins. Then test the path when people are tired, rushed, or distracted, because that is when the lower-energy route shows itself. A system will usually follow the cheaper path, so make the cheaper path worthy of being followed.

examples.title: Louise Moves the Tax Folder

planSpec.audience: readers who face tax filing default folder decisions where energy output is easy to misread
planSpec.requiredBeat: Louise moves the better action onto the tax folder, removes the easier bad path from the deduction receipt, and checks the filing checklist to confirm low effort now serves the goal. Domain: tax filing default folder.

examples.scenario: The tax folder lies open on Louise's desk while a deduction receipt curls beside the old drawer after a long commute. "I always mean to file it," she says, holding the checklist and looking at the hallway table where mail lands. Louise must choose the environment: keep the closer drawer, or make the folder the first place her hand can go.
examples.whatToDo: Put the tax folder in the receipt path, clip the filing checklist to it, and move the old drawer farther away.
examples.whyItMatters: The lower-energy path was scattering documents. The fix makes the easiest motion serve filing.

examples.title: Brian Flips the Scanner Strap

planSpec.audience: readers who face warehouse picker route decisions where energy output is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: workers walking extra steps all shift
planSpec.requiredBeat: Brian moves the better action onto the aisle map, removes the easier bad path from the scanner strap, and checks the step counter to confirm low effort now serves the goal. Domain: warehouse picker route.

examples.scenario: "The route is on the map," Brian says, watching the step counter climb near the loading dock. The scanner strap sits on the side that makes the old loop easier to scan, even though the aisle map shows a shorter turn. Before the next shift, he has to decide between blaming pickers and flipping the strap so the shorter aisle route becomes the natural motion.
examples.whatToDo: Move the scanner strap and aisle map cues so the shortest route requires fewer steps and fewer reaches.
examples.whyItMatters: Workers followed the easier physical path. Changing friction did more than asking for discipline.

examples.title: Remy Fills the Prep Tray

planSpec.audience: readers who face meal prep station setup decisions where energy output is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: healthy dinners failing on tired evenings
planSpec.requiredBeat: Remy moves the better action onto the prep tray, removes the easier bad path from the recipe card, and checks the freezer label to confirm low effort now serves the goal. Domain: meal prep station setup.

examples.scenario: The kitchen counter is clean, the prep tray is empty, and the recipe card asks for chopping after work when Remy is already hungry. He predicts care will carry him through dinner. The reveal comes at 7:30: the freezer label hides ready ingredients while delivery takes two taps. He must decide which path gets the lower effort.
examples.whatToDo: Put chopped ingredients on the prep tray, label the freezer clearly, and make the delivery path less immediate.
examples.whyItMatters: Healthy dinner failed because it cost more energy at the tired moment. The better default had to become easier.

examples.title: Brianna Locks the First Ten Minutes

planSpec.audience: readers who face study app notification defaults decisions where energy output is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: study opening displaced by the phone
planSpec.requiredBeat: Brianna moves the better action onto the notification screen, removes the easier bad path from the practice deck, and checks the lockout setting to confirm low effort now serves the goal. Domain: study app notification defaults.

examples.scenario: At 11:04 p.m., Brianna opens the notification screen after the practice deck loses again, with tomorrow's quiz still in the corner of her notebook. Every message reached her before the first study card did. In the postmortem, she stops calling it weak focus and sets a lockout that makes the first ten minutes of practice the easiest next action.
examples.whatToDo: Set the lockout before opening the practice deck and place the deck on the first screen after unlock.
examples.whyItMatters: Attention followed the cheaper path. The default had to make study easier than checking messages.

examples.title: Samuel Removes Mark Later

planSpec.audience: readers who face payroll approval shortcut decisions where energy output is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: late payments caused by one click
planSpec.requiredBeat: Samuel moves the better action onto the approval queue, removes the easier bad path from the invoice timestamp, and checks the vendor email to confirm low effort now serves the goal. Domain: payroll approval shortcut.

examples.scenario: You see Samuel's approval queue beside a vendor email marked urgent, with the invoice timestamp already four days old. The easiest button says "mark later," and the actual approval requires two screens. Samuel hovers over two paths: preserve the shortcut that creates late payments, or make the next valid approval the one-click action.
examples.whatToDo: Remove the mark-later shortcut for valid invoices and surface the next approvable item in the queue.
examples.whyItMatters: The system conserved effort by delaying work. Moving ease to approval reduced late-payment drift.

examples.title: Rafael Moves the Lint Bin

planSpec.audience: readers who face apartment laundry sorting system decisions where energy output is easy to misread
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rafael moves the better action onto the lint sign, removes the easier bad path from the sorting shelf, and checks the laundry token to confirm low effort now serves the goal. Domain: apartment laundry sorting system.

examples.scenario: It took Rafael three laundry cycles to notice the lint sign was in the wrong place, taped above a sorting shelf nobody faced after drying. The shelf blocked the small bin, and the laundry token machine pulled neighbors toward the exit. He must choose between another warning and moving the cleanup cue into the lowest-effort path.
examples.whatToDo: Put the lint bin beside the dryer door and move the sign to the token machine so cleanup happens before exit.
examples.whyItMatters: People were not uniquely careless. The room made leaving easier than cleaning, so the environment needed redesign.

questions.prompt: Receipts keep landing in a hallway drawer after work because the tax folder is farther away and the filing checklist is hidden. What is the energy-output move?
choices: Move the folder and checklist into the receipt path.
Call the person lazy for using the drawer.
Make filing more complicated to prove commitment.
questions.explanation: The easier path is currently the drawer. Moving the folder into the path makes the lower-effort action serve filing.

questions.prompt: Warehouse pickers follow an old walking loop all shift because the scanner strap makes that loop easiest, even though the aisle map shows a shorter route. What should change?
choices: Tell pickers to try harder while keeping the same setup.
Move scanner and map cues so the shorter route costs less effort.
Ignore step counts because walking is part of the job.
questions.explanation: The path of least resistance is physical. Changing the strap and cues lowers energy for the desired route.

questions.prompt: A healthy dinner plan fails after work because chopping starts from zero while delivery takes two taps on a tired evening. Which action fits the model?
choices: Make the recipe harder to prove discipline.
Blame tiredness and change nothing.
Prepare the tray and freezer labels so cooking is the lowest-effort path.
questions.explanation: At the tired moment, effort decides. Prep and labels make the desired dinner cheaper than delivery.

questions.prompt: A study app loses to notifications because messages appear before the first practice card during the opening ten minutes. What is the best redesign?
choices: Tell the student to care more.
Set a lockout and place the practice deck as the first available action.
Add more notifications about studying.
questions.explanation: The phone made distraction lower effort than practice. Lockout and deck placement reverse the default.

questions.prompt: A payroll queue has a one-click 'mark later' button, and valid invoices age for days until vendors complain by email. What is the strongest diagnosis?
choices: Vendors are too impatient.
Approvers need a longer policy document.
The system made delay cheaper than approval.
questions.explanation: The shortcut channels effort toward delay. Removing it and surfacing approvable invoices makes completion cheaper.

questions.prompt: Neighbors leave lint traps full because the small bin is blocked by the sorting shelf and the token machine pulls them toward the exit. What should the landlord change?
choices: Move the bin and cleanup cue into the exit path before the token step.
Post a longer angry sign in the same place.
Assume every neighbor is careless.
questions.explanation: The room made leaving easier than cleaning. Redesigning the path changes effort instead of relying on shame.

questions.prompt: A manager says harder work is always better and adds steps to every quality process. Errors rise because rushed staff skip the process. What went wrong?
choices: The manager worshiped effort instead of designing the low-energy path to support quality.
Quality processes should never exist.
Skipping proves workers cannot improve.
questions.explanation: Higher effort can drive avoidance. The model asks you to aim ease toward the goal, not make every good action harder.

questions.prompt: A clinic puts hand sanitizer directly in the doorway and moves empty stands away from desks. Use rises without reminders during patient intake. How should you evaluate this?
choices: It fails because people did not prove discipline.
It likely works because the desired action became the lower-effort path.
It proves reminders are always useless.
questions.explanation: The environment made the desired behavior easier. The model explains why placement can outperform exhortation.

questions.prompt: A family wants fewer missed bills, but paper mail lands on a hallway shelf while the bill folder is upstairs in a closed cabinet. Which response transfers the model?
choices: Promise to climb upstairs every day.
Hide the mail so it looks cleaner.
Place the bill folder at the mail drop and move unrelated clutter away.
questions.explanation: The good action must be the cheaper action. Putting the folder at the mail drop makes sorting easier than postponing.

reviewCards.front: A repeated behavior looks like laziness. What should you retrieve first?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve energy minimization: inspect which path costs less effort before judging character.

reviewCards.front: A shortcut keeps winning before anyone thinks. What should you retrieve about the default?
reviewCards.back: The default is the low-effort path the environment makes easiest to follow.

reviewCards.front: A good action takes three more motions than the bad path. How do you make it more likely?
reviewCards.back: Remove motions from the good path and add friction to the harmful path.

reviewCards.front: A quality process gets harder and people skip it. Why can harder work backfire?
reviewCards.back: Extra effort can make people avoid the process, turning quality into a conservation trap.

reviewCards.front: A product can make any behavior easier. What is the ethical use of effort reduction?
reviewCards.back: Aim ease toward actions you can defend, because systems usually follow the cheaper path.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to make the lower-effort path serve the goal. The skill is moving friction and defaults instead of worshiping effort.

ifThenPlans.plan: If documents scatter, then I will place the correct folder at the first drop point.
If workers take the longer route, then I will inspect which route requires fewer motions before blaming behavior.
If an app displaces the intended action, then I will make the intended action first and add lockout friction to the distraction.
If cleanup is skipped, then I will move the bin, sign, or tool into the natural exit path.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, choose one repeated failure. Remove two motions from the desired action and add one motion to the easier bad path.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, audit one default by asking: which path costs less energy, what goal it serves, and what friction should move.

memorableLines.text: The default is the real instruction.
memorableLines.why: It makes environmental design more concrete than intention.

memorableLines.text: Design beats scolding when the easier path is wrong.
memorableLines.why: It rejects the laziness misread in a short form.

memorableLines.text: The work is not to make life harder. The work is to aim ease.
memorableLines.why: It closes the model with the practical design principle.
